title: What is DCF?
subtitle: Valuing a company as the present value of all its future cash flows
openingQuestion: What core principle from the Time Value of Money track does the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) method rest on?
openingOptions: The current book value of assets on the balance sheet
Comparison with similar companies in the market
The average share price over the past 12 months
A business's value equals the total present value (Present Value) of all the free cash flow it will generate in the future, discounted back to today at a rate reflecting risk and cost of capital
explanation: DCF (Discounted Cash Flow) is an ABSOLUTE valuation method (intrinsic valuation): forecast the Free Cash Flow the company will generate over the coming years, discount it back to present value using WACC (weighted average cost of capital), and add the present value of the Terminal Value (the value of everything after the forecast period). It is the most theoretically 'pure' method because it does not depend on how the market prices the company or its peers.

diagram.label: Forecast free cash flow for 5-10 years
Calculate a terminal value for everything after
Discount everything back to today using WACC
Get enterprise value, subtract net debt for equity value

realWorldExample.description: Serious analysts often build detailed 5-10 year DCF models for companies with forecastable cash flows (such as consumer or telecom companies) to get a view of value independent of short-term market sentiment swings.

quiz.question: Why is DCF considered an 'absolute' valuation method while Comps and Precedent Transaction are 'relative'?
options: Because DCF can only be applied to companies already listed on an exchange
Because DCF builds value from the company's own fundamentals, not by referencing other companies
Because DCF requires no assumptions at all about the future, so the result is fully objective
Because DCF always produces an absolutely accurate result in every case and industry
quiz.explanation: Comps and Precedent Transaction are both RELATIVE valuations - based on how the market prices other companies. DCF is ABSOLUTE valuation - it builds value entirely from the company's own fundamentals (cash flow forecast, specific risk, cost of capital).

quiz.question: An analyst builds two DCF models for the same company, differing only in the assumed 5-year revenue growth rate (8% vs 12%). How much can the valuation results differ, and what does that say about the nature of DCF?
options: The results are identical since only one small assumption differs
DCF always gives an accurate result regardless of which input assumptions are used
The gap can be very large (20-50%+) - DCF reflects the quality of its assumptions
Revenue growth has no meaningful effect on the DCF result
quiz.explanation: This is a key fact to remember about DCF: "garbage in, garbage out" - the accuracy of the result depends entirely on the quality of the input assumptions, not on the formula itself.

quiz.question: What three inputs determine the result of a DCF model?
options: Industry multiple, growth rate, and dividend payout ratio
Revenue, cost, and profit over the last three years
Share price, shares outstanding, and net debt
Forecast cash flow, discount rate, and terminal value
quiz.explanation: These three inputs drive almost the entire result, and all three are estimates. This is why DCF is sometimes called falsely precise - a rigorous calculation performed on numbers nobody can know for certain.

quiz.question: Why is DCF called an absolute valuation while Comps is called relative?
options: Because DCF is calculated from that company's own cash flow
Because DCF always produces a more accurate result than Comps
Because DCF requires no assumptions at all about the future
Because Comps can only be used for companies already listed
quiz.explanation: DCF doesn't ask what the market is currently paying for someone else. It builds value from the cash flow the business itself will generate - so it can still give an answer even when the whole industry is being mispriced.

quiz.question: Two DCF models of the same company give results that differ by 40%. What is the most common cause?
options: One of the two models added up its cash flows incorrectly
They differ in the WACC and perpetual growth assumptions
The two models used two different accounting standards
One model uses cash flow while the other uses profit
quiz.explanation: DCF is highly sensitive to these two assumptions because both sit in the denominator of the Terminal Value, which accounts for 60-80% of the result. A one-percentage-point difference there is enough to produce a gap of tens of percent.

keyTakeaways: DCF: enterprise value = the total present value of future free cash flow
An absolute valuation method, independent of how the market prices other companies
Accuracy depends heavily on the quality of the cash flow forecast and discount rate assumptions

practicePrompt.question: An analyst forecasts a company's free cash flow (FCF) for the next 10 years, estimates a Terminal Value for everything after, then discounts it all back to today using WACC to arrive at a single enterprise value figure. What is this valuation method called?
options: This is the Comps method, since it compares the company against other companies in the market
DCF: enterprise value = the total present value of future free cash flow
This is the Precedent Transaction method, since it is based on past M&A deals
This isn't really a valuation method at all, just a plain financial forecasting model
practicePrompt.explanation: DCF: enterprise value = the total present value of future free cash flow. This is an intrinsic valuation method - it does not depend on the market price of other companies, but on the company's own ability to generate cash.

summary.keyIdea: DCF: enterprise value = the total present value of future free cash flow
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a definition to recite rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: An absolute valuation method, independent of how the market prices other companies

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: For a company whose business model you understand well, try a rough sketch: what is next year's free cash flow roughly likely to be, and is it trending up or down over the next few years, in your own judgement.
application.secondary: No need to be precise yet - just build the habit of thinking about future cash flow instead of just looking at price.

sections.text: While Comps and Precedent Transaction ask 'what is the market currently paying for similar companies', DCF asks a completely different question: based on the cash flow it generates, what is this company itself actually worth?
The structure of a DCF model

DCF (Discounted Cash Flow) is an ABSOLUTE valuation method: forecast the Free Cash Flow the company will generate over the coming years, discount it back to present value using WACC (weighted average cost of capital), and add the present value of the Terminal Value (representing everything after the forecast period). Analysts often build detailed 5-10 year DCF models for companies with forecastable cash flows, to get a view of value independent of short-term market sentiment swings.
Why DCF is 'absolute' and Comps is 'relative'

DCF builds value entirely from the company's own fundamentals (cash flow, specific risk, cost of capital), without referencing the price of any other company in the market. This is why DCF is useful for spotting when the whole market is mispriced. But remember: DCF is extremely sensitive to assumptions. Simply changing the 5-year revenue growth assumption from 8% to 12% can shift the valuation result by 20-50% or more - DCF is not a 'precise value calculator' but a tool that directly reflects the quality and reasonableness of the assumptions fed into it.

items: DCF is independent of market pricing - useful for spotting systematic mispricing
Extremely sensitive to growth, margin, and WACC assumptions
"Garbage in, garbage out" - the result is only as good as the input assumptions
Should always be accompanied by a sensitivity analysis when presenting DCF results

lines: DCF doesn't give you an absolutely correct number - it gives you a framework for understanding what a company is worth, if your assumptions are right.
